title: Manage volunteers in an extension project or event

lessons.title: Planning for volunteers
lessons.html:
Volunteers in extension work

Many extension projects and events rely on volunteers: lead farmers who share knowledge with neighbours, youth who help register participants at an agricultural show, community members who assist at a vaccination campaign or a farmer day, and retired farmers who mentor new entrants. Volunteers extend the reach of limited staff and budgets and strengthen community ownership. However, volunteers are not free labour. They need planning, support and recognition, or they will leave and the project will suffer.

Deciding where volunteers can help

Start by listing the project's tasks and deciding which are suitable for volunteers. Suitable tasks are meaningful, clearly defined and match the skills and time volunteers can offer. Tasks requiring professional responsibility, such as giving veterinary treatment, applying restricted chemicals or handling large sums of money, should remain with qualified staff or be closely supervised.

Writing volunteer role descriptions

For each role, write a short description including:

  • Role title and purpose, for example: registration volunteer at a farmer day.
  • Tasks and responsibilities.
  • Skills or experience needed, such as speaking isiXhosa and English or basic computer use.
  • Time commitment, dates and hours.
  • Who supervises the volunteer.
  • Support provided, such as training, meals, transport and a T-shirt.

Policies and risk

Your organisation should have a volunteer policy covering recruitment, screening, conduct, safety, reimbursement of expenses, insurance and confidentiality. Identify risks to volunteers and to the public. Where volunteers handle animals, machinery, crowds or work outdoors in heat, plan safety measures and briefings. Where they work with children or vulnerable people, follow screening requirements set by your organisation.

Budget for volunteer costs. Transport, refreshments, training materials and recognition items cost money, and failing to provide them damages goodwill. Clarify whether any stipend is paid, and get advice from your HR function so that volunteer arrangements are not confused with employment.

lessons.title: Recruiting, selecting and preparing volunteers
lessons.html:
Finding the right people

Recruit through channels your target volunteers trust and use: farmer association meetings, church and community gatherings, schools and agricultural colleges, youth organisations, WhatsApp groups, community radio and word of mouth from existing volunteers. Explain clearly what the role involves, the time commitment and what volunteers will gain, such as skills, experience for their CV, a certificate, networking or simply contributing to their community.

Selection

Hold a short conversation with each candidate to discuss their interests, skills and availability. Match people to roles that suit them. A respected older farmer might be an excellent lead farmer for a demonstration plot, while a tech-savvy student might manage registrations on a tablet. Be honest if a role does not fit someone, and offer an alternative where possible. Apply any screening your organisation requires.

Orientation and training

Every volunteer needs orientation before starting:

  1. Background: the project's purpose, the organisation and how their role fits.
  2. Role briefing: exactly what to do, where, when and with whom.
  3. Conduct: respectful behaviour, dress, confidentiality of farmer information and what to do if approached by the media.
  4. Safety: hazards on site, PPE where relevant, emergency procedures, location of first aid and who to report incidents to. Volunteers should not provide first aid unless they have been trained by an accredited provider.
  5. Practical skills: hands-on practice, for example using the registration form or setting up a demonstration plot.

Give volunteers a contact person and phone number, a schedule and any materials in writing. For larger events, run a short briefing session on the morning itself to confirm arrangements and answer questions.

Keep a volunteer register with names, contact details, emergency contacts, roles, training completed and hours contributed. This information supports planning, reporting to funders and recognition.

lessons.title: Supervising, motivating and recognising volunteers
lessons.html:
Support during the project or event

Supervision of volunteers should be supportive rather than controlling. Assign a coordinator for each team. Check in regularly, answer questions and solve problems quickly. Make sure volunteers have water, shade, meals and rest breaks, particularly at outdoor events such as field days or livestock auctions. Monitor safety continuously and stop any unsafe activity.

Motivating volunteers

People volunteer for different reasons: helping the community, learning skills, meeting people, gaining experience or status. Find out what motivates each volunteer and try to meet those needs. Motivation grows when volunteers:

  • Understand how their work contributes to the project's results.
  • Are trusted with real responsibility.
  • Receive feedback and appreciation.
  • Have opportunities to learn and take on new roles.
  • Feel treated fairly and with respect.

Handling problems

Problems may include volunteers not arriving, poor performance, conflict with staff or farmers, or inappropriate behaviour. Address issues privately and respectfully, find out the cause and agree on a solution. Sometimes moving a volunteer to a more suitable role solves the problem. Where conduct is serious, such as harassment or dishonesty, follow your organisation's volunteer policy, which may include ending the volunteer's involvement.

Recognition and review

Recognition keeps volunteers returning. Thank volunteers personally and publicly, for example at the closing of a farmer day. Provide certificates, letters of reference or small tokens of appreciation. Share project results so that volunteers see their impact.

After the project or event, hold a debriefing with volunteers. Ask what went well, what was difficult and what could improve. Record hours contributed and lessons learnt. Update the volunteer register and keep in touch with good volunteers for future projects.

Key points

  • Volunteers need planning, support and recognition; they are not free labour.
  • Write clear role descriptions and keep professional tasks with qualified staff.
  • Recruit through trusted channels and match people to suitable roles.
  • Orientate every volunteer on purpose, role, conduct and safety.
  • Supervise supportively, address problems early and recognise contributions.
